justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term trajectory with modest upward drift over time. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 585 was anchored heavily on the most recent observed value and short-term momentum, assuming continuity in whatever process or market was being tracked. The one-week estimate of 588 incorporates a slight upward drift, acknowledging that mean-reversion pressures were weak and the prevailing trend was mildly positive. The one-month estimate of 595 extends that drift further while also pulling slightly toward a longer-run equilibrium level, reflecting the assumption that whatever near-term forces are at play will partially fade but not fully reverse over a four-week window.

The confidence interval widths expand meaningfully as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the compounding of uncertainty over time. At one day, the interval of roughly plus or minus 17 units is tight because there is little time for new information or shocks to accumulate. By one week, the interval widens to plus or minus 33 units, incorporating the possibility of mid-week data releases, sentiment shifts, or technical level breaks. At one month, the interval of plus or minus 65 units reflects the realistic possibility of regime changes, macro surprises, or sustained trend reversals that simply cannot be predicted at shorter horizons.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected negative macro shock — such as a sharp deterioration in economic data, a policy surprise, or a liquidity event — could easily drive the value below the lower bound of the one-month interval around 530. On the upside, a strong catalyst such as better-than-expected fundamental news or a broader risk-on sentiment surge could push the value above 660. These tail risks are by definition underweighted in my intervals, which are designed to capture the central 90% of outcomes rather than extreme scenarios.

It is also worth noting that the intervals assume relatively stable volatility across the forecast period. If realized volatility spikes — as it tends to during earnings seasons, geopolitical events, or central bank surprises — the true distribution of outcomes would be heavier-tailed than my intervals suggest. Conversely, if conditions remain unusually calm and range-bound, the actual outcome could land well inside even my tightest interval. Forecasters should treat the one-month interval in particular with humility, as a great deal can change over thirty days that no model fully anticipates.
